sentences.text: The length of the Dakotaraptor thighbone is 558 mm.
The prominent bumps on the ulna are called ulnar papillae or quill knobs, which served as attachment points for wing feathers.
The back vertebrae were highly pneumatized, filled with trabecular bone containing many air spaces.
Dakotaraptor likely had a furcula shaped between a U and V, similar to many dromaeosaurids like Velociraptor and the large spinosaurid Suchomimus.
Generally, the hind limbs were of light constitution with long bone elements, unlike the robust limbs of Utahraptor.
Dakotaraptor had a reduced protuberance for the flexor tendon attachment on the fourth toe claw.
Dakotaraptor was one of the largest dromaeosaurids, with estimates of 4.35 to 6 meters in length and 220 to 350 kilograms in weight.
Adult Dakotaraptor individuals were too heavy to fly, yet their feathers were not reduced despite this flightless condition.
The genus Dakotaraptor was described by DePalma and colleagues in 2015.
Paleontologist Robert DePalma discovered the site yielding Dakotaraptor remains in Harding County, South Dakota, in 2005.
The species Dakotaraptor steini was formally named and described in 2015 by DePalma, Burnham, Martin, Larson, and Bakker.
The holotype was found in sandstone layers from the upper part of the Hell Creek Formation, dating to the late Maastrichtian.
The holotype consists of a partial adult skeleton lacking a skull.
Wide ulnar papillae for the calaminae of large pennaceous feathers were located on the ulna in the forearm.
Adult individuals of Dakotaraptor were too heavy to fly.
Possible functions for the wings include egg protection, display, intimidation, and maintaining balance while attacking prey with the killing claw.
Bone histology studies showed that both the robust and gracile morphs were adults, meaning the light bone constitution was not due to a juvenile stage.
While pathologies or individual variation could explain the difference, the simplest explanation is sexual dimorphism.
It cannot yet be deduced which morph was male and which was female.
Dakotaraptor was placed in Dromaeosauridae, and a cladistic analysis showed it was the sister taxon of Dromaeosaurus.
A 2019 study by Hartman et al. recovered a placement of Dakotaraptor in Unenlagiidae.
Dakotaraptor is classified within the family Dromaeosauridae.
A 2019 study suggests that Dakotaraptor is likely a member of the subfamily Unenlagiinae.
The genus authority for Dakotaraptor is DePalma et al., 2015.
The species authority for Dakotaraptor steini is DePalma et al., 2015.
Dakotaraptor lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Maastrichtian age.
Dakotaraptor lived during the Maastrichtian stage, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
Remains found in the Maastrichtian-aged Hell Creek Formation suggest Dakotaraptor was potentially one of the last surviving dromaeosaurids, a classification disputed by other researchers.
By 2024, some dinosaurian elements of Dakotaraptor were questioned, as traits thought diagnostic for dromaeosaurs were also found in caenagnathids and ornithomimosaurians.
In 2015, researchers suggested that the alleged furculae of Dakotaraptor actually represented part of a turtle shell, specifically the entoplastron of Axestemys splendida.
The authors of its description considered it probable that Dakotaraptor descended from a small gliding ancestor that possessed these papillae.
